block/plain: A plain layer replaces its input with something new. A residual block keeps its input, x, and adds a change to it.
block/add: The layers inside, a conv, a ReLU and another conv, compute a function of x, written F of x. Here F names that function, not a filter size. A shortcut carries x around them, and the two are added: y equals x plus F of x.
block/example: If x is two, minus one and three, and F gives a half, a half and minus one, then y is two and a half, minus a half, and two.
block/zero: To leave its input alone, a block only has to make F zero. So an extra block need not make the network worse.
match/need: The sum needs x and F of x in the same shape. Take an x with sixty four channels, eight by eight: sixty four by eight by eight.
match/keep: If F's convs have sixty four filters, stride one and padding one, F of x has that shape too, and the shortcut is x itself.
match/first: Now give F's first conv a hundred and twenty eight filters, and stride two. A hundred and twenty eight filters make a hundred and twenty eight channels.
match/round: Its width: eight minus three, plus two for the padding, over two, plus one. That is four and a half. It is not whole, so it rounds down: four.
match/second: The second conv, stride one and padding one, keeps four by four. So F of x is a hundred and twenty eight by four by four, and x cannot be added to it.
match/cut: So the shortcut becomes a one by one conv, with F's channels, a hundred and twenty eight filters, and F's stride, two.
match/check: Its width, with no padding: eight minus one, over two, plus one, is four and a half again, so four. The shortcut gives a hundred and twenty eight by four by four, and the sum works.
gradient/split: Going backward, the sum is an add gate: it hands the gradient arriving at y, g, to both of its inputs.
gradient/paths: Along the shortcut, g reaches x unchanged. Through F, it gets multiplied by F's slope, F prime.
gradient/formula: The two paths add up at x: g times one plus F prime. With g equal to two and a slope of a half, that is three.
gradient/stack: Now stack two blocks. The first turns x into h, through layers F one. The second turns h into y, through layers F two.
gradient/back2: Walking back, each block multiplies the gradient by one plus its slope. Say g is one, and F two prime is one: block two hands h one times two, which is two.
gradient/back1: Block one, with F one prime at minus a half, hands x two times a half: one. The blocks are in a chain, so their factors multiply.
gradient/deep: Now stack fifty layers. If each one halves the gradient, almost nothing reaches the first. With shortcuts, each block multiplies by one plus a slope, so the gradient arrives intact.
